nodes.label: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, Chapter 1
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Chapter goal is a big-picture vocabulary of the Internet, protocols, edge and core, performance, layering, security, and history, with depth deferred to later chapters.

nodes.label: Internet
nodes.rationale: Nuts-and-bolts view: a network of networks of hosts, packet switches, and links managed by organizations. Services view: infrastructure for networked applications plus a programming interface, analogous to the postal service, that lets distributed apps send and receive using a transport service.

nodes.label: Protocol
nodes.rationale: Protocols define the format and order of messages sent and received among network entities and the actions taken on transmission, receipt, or other events. All Internet communication is governed by protocols.

nodes.label: Host (End System)
nodes.rationale: Hosts are end systems running network applications at the Internet edge, acting as clients and servers. Servers often sit in data centers. A sending host breaks an application message into packets of L bits and transmits them into the access network at link rate R.

nodes.label: Packet Switch
nodes.rationale: Routers and switches forward packets. In the end-to-end encapsulation picture a router handles headers through the network layer, while a switch handles link and physical headers.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.rationale: Application protocol for the Web. The running example is a GET of http://gaia.cs.umass.edu/kurose_ross after a TCP connection handshake. History credits HTML and HTTP to Berners-Lee.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.rationale: Transport protocol providing process-to-process transfer. The protocol walk-through shows a TCP connection request and response before the application exchange. TCP congestion control was added in 1988 because packet switching can congest.

nodes.label: IP
nodes.rationale: Network-layer protocol that carries datagrams from source host to destination host. DNS maps names to IP addresses.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.rationale: Application-layer protocol defined in 1983 for name-to-IP-address translation.

nodes.label: Ethernet
nodes.rationale: Wired link technology: enterprise access at 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, and 10 Gbps, and twisted-pair categories cited for 100 Mbps through 10 Gbps Ethernet. Developed at Xerox PARC in 1976. Shared Ethernet is a broadcast medium that enables packet sniffing.

nodes.label: WiFi (IEEE 802.11)
nodes.rationale: Wireless LAN within or around a building. End systems reach a router via a base station (access point). Cited rates include 11, 54, and 450 Mbps for 802.11b/g/n. Shared wireless media can be sniffed.

nodes.label: Network Edge
nodes.rationale: The edge is hosts (clients and servers, servers often in data centers) plus the access networks and physical media that connect them to the core.

nodes.label: Access Network
nodes.rationale: Connects end systems to an edge router. Residential access uses cable or DSL; institutional access mixes Ethernet and WiFi; mobile access uses WiFi and 4G/5G. A home network often combines a cable or DSL modem with a router, firewall, and NAT, plus wired Ethernet and a WiFi access point.

nodes.label: Hybrid Fiber Coax (HFC)
nodes.rationale: Cable access sends data and TV at different frequencies over a shared cable distribution network. Asymmetric: about 40 Mbps to 1.2 Gbps downstream and 30-100 Mbps upstream. Homes share the path to the cable headend and CMTS, which attaches to the ISP.

nodes.label: Digital Subscriber Line (DSL)
nodes.rationale: Uses the existing telephone line to a central-office DSLAM. Voice and data travel at different frequencies on a dedicated line, so the access line is not shared among homes the way cable is. Cited rates are 24-52 Mbps downstream and 3.5-16 Mbps upstream. Data goes to the Internet and voice to the telephone network.

nodes.label: Physical Media
nodes.rationale: Guided media (twisted pair, coax, fiber) carry signals in a solid; unguided radio propagates freely and is affected by reflection, obstruction, and interference. Fiber offers tens to hundreds of Gbps and low error rates because it is immune to electromagnetic noise. Radio types include WiFi, 4G/5G, Bluetooth, terrestrial microwave, and satellite (geostationary delay about 270 ms; Starlink cited for downlink).

nodes.label: Network Core
nodes.rationale: Mesh of interconnected routers that forwards packets hop by hop from source to destination. Two key functions are forwarding (local) and routing (global).

nodes.label: Packet Switching
nodes.rationale: Hosts break application messages into packets that routers forward. Suited to bursty data because of statistical resource sharing and no call setup. A 1 Gb/s link with users active 10% of the time at 100 Mb/s can admit far more than the 10 circuit-switched users; with 35 users the chance more than 10 are active is under 0.0004. Congestion can cause delay and loss, so reliable transfer and congestion control are needed. Making packet switching behave like circuits is described as complicated.

nodes.label: Circuit Switching
nodes.rationale: End-to-end resources are reserved for a call, giving guaranteed circuit-like performance, but an idle circuit is not shared. Common in traditional telephone networks. Implemented by FDM or TDM. On the example 1 Gb/s link, circuit switching supports 10 users who each need 100 Mb/s.

nodes.label: Forwarding
nodes.rationale: Also called switching. Local action: move an arriving packet from the router's input link to the output link selected by a local forwarding table indexed by the destination address in the packet header.

nodes.label: Routing
nodes.rationale: Global action: routing algorithms determine the source-destination paths packets take. Cerf and Kahn's architecture uses stateless routing and decentralized control.

nodes.label: Store-and-Forward
nodes.rationale: The entire packet must arrive at a router before it can be transmitted on the next link. Pushing an L-bit packet onto a link of rate R takes L/R seconds. Example: L = 10 Kbits and R = 100 Mbps gives a one-hop transmission delay of 0.1 ms.

nodes.label: Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM)
nodes.rationale: Divides a link into frequency bands so each call transmits continuously at the rate of its narrow band. Cable access also uses FDM so video and data occupy different channels on a shared coax plant.

nodes.label: Time Division Multiplexing (TDM)
nodes.rationale: Divides time into slots. Each call gets periodic slots and may transmit at the full wider-band rate only during its slot.

nodes.label: Internet Service Provider (ISP)
nodes.rationale: Hosts connect through access ISPs, which must be interconnected so any two hosts can exchange packets. A full mesh of access ISPs is O(N^2) and does not scale. One global transit ISP works commercially, then competitors appear, then peering, regional ISPs, and content-provider networks. Evolution is driven by economics and national policy. Customer and provider ISPs have an economic agreement.

nodes.label: Internet Exchange Point (IXP)
nodes.rationale: Competing global ISPs interconnect at Internet exchange points over peering links rather than only through a single transit provider.

nodes.label: Tier-1 ISP
nodes.rationale: A small number of well-connected commercial ISPs (examples: Level 3, Sprint, AT&T, NTT) with national and international coverage sit at the center of the Internet.

nodes.label: Content Provider Network
nodes.rationale: Providers such as Google, Microsoft, Akamai, and Facebook run private networks that connect their data centers to the Internet, often bypassing tier-1 and regional ISPs, so content is close to end users.

nodes.label: Nodal Delay
nodes.rationale: Total nodal delay is dnodal = dproc + dqueue + dtrans + dprop. Transmission delay and propagation delay are different quantities; the caravan analogy separates time to push the packet onto the link from time for bits to travel to the next node.

nodes.label: Processing Delay
nodes.rationale: Time to check bit errors and choose the output link. Typically under a microsecond.

nodes.label: Queueing Delay
nodes.rationale: Time waiting at an output link when packets arrive faster than the link can send them. Depends on congestion. Traffic intensity La/R near 0 means small average delay, near 1 means large delay, and above 1 means more work arrives than can be served so average delay is infinite.

nodes.label: Transmission Delay
nodes.rationale: Time to push an L-bit packet onto a link of transmission rate R: dtrans = L/R. Link transmission rate is also called link capacity or bandwidth.

nodes.label: Propagation Delay
nodes.rationale: Time for a bit to travel a physical link of length d at propagation speed s (about 2×10^8 m/s): dprop = d/s. Distinct from transmission delay.

nodes.label: Packet Loss
nodes.rationale: Router buffers are finite. If the arrival rate to a link exceeds its transmission rate long enough for the buffer to fill, arriving packets are dropped. A lost packet may be retransmitted by the previous node, by the source end system, or not at all.

nodes.label: Throughput
nodes.rationale: Rate at which bits are delivered from sender to receiver, instantaneous or average. Average end-end throughput is limited by the bottleneck link. With server link Rs, client link Rc, and n connections sharing a backbone of rate R, per-connection throughput is min(Rc, Rs, R/n). In practice Rc or Rs is often the bottleneck.

nodes.label: Traceroute
nodes.rationale: Measures delay from a source to each router along the path toward a destination. For hop i it sends three probes whose time-to-live is i; router i returns the packets and the sender records the interval. A star means no response. The chapter's example is gaia.cs.umass.edu to www.eurecom.fr, including a trans-oceanic link.

nodes.label: Network Security
nodes.rationale: The Internet was not originally designed with much security; the original vision was mutually trusting users on a transparent network, so designers later played catch-up and put security considerations in all layers. Defenses named here: authentication (a SIM gives hardware identity in cellular networks; the traditional Internet has no such assist), confidentiality via encryption, integrity via digital signatures, password-protected VPNs, and firewalls. Deeper treatment is deferred to Chapter 8.

nodes.label: Packet Sniffing
nodes.rationale: On broadcast media (shared Ethernet, wireless), a promiscuous interface can read and record every packet that passes, including passwords. Wireshark is the packet sniffer used in the end-of-chapter labs; the closing slide shows it capturing a copy of Ethernet frames.

nodes.label: IP Spoofing
nodes.rationale: Injection of a packet with a false source address so the sender claims another host's identity.

nodes.label: Denial of Service (DoS)
nodes.rationale: Attackers make a server or bandwidth unavailable to legitimate traffic by overwhelming it with bogus traffic. The chapter's sketch is: select a target, compromise hosts around the network (a botnet), and send packets to the target from those hosts.

nodes.label: Firewall
nodes.rationale: Specialized middlebox in access and core networks. Off-by-default filtering of incoming packets restricts senders, receivers, and applications, and is also a place to detect or react to denial-of-service attacks. Home access devices often combine the router, firewall, and NAT.

nodes.label: Internet Protocol Stack
nodes.rationale: Layering organizes a complex system: each layer implements a service by its own actions while relying on the layer below. Explicit structure makes the pieces and their relationships discussable, and modularization lets one layer's implementation change transparently to the rest of the system. The Internet stack has five layers: application, transport, network, link, and physical.

nodes.label: Application Layer
nodes.rationale: Supports network applications. Named protocols include HTTP, IMAP, SMTP, and DNS. Applications exchange messages using the transport layer's service. OSI presentation and session services, if needed, are implemented here because the Internet stack has no separate layers for them.

nodes.label: Transport Layer
nodes.rationale: Process-to-process data transfer, exemplified by TCP and UDP. Encapsulates the application message M with header Ht to form a segment, and transfers that message using the network layer, reliably in the TCP case.

nodes.label: Network Layer
nodes.rationale: Routes datagrams from source to destination using IP and routing protocols. Encapsulates the transport segment with header Hn and transfers it host-to-host using link-layer services.

nodes.label: Link Layer
nodes.rationale: Transfers data between neighboring network elements. Named technologies: Ethernet, 802.11 WiFi, and PPP. Encapsulates the datagram with header Hl to form a frame and moves that frame to the next host using the physical layer.

nodes.label: Physical Layer
nodes.rationale: Moves bits on the wire between a transmitter and a receiver.

nodes.label: Encapsulation
nodes.rationale: Each layer wraps the unit from above with its own header so it can implement its service: application message M, transport segment Ht+M, network datagram Hn+segment, link frame Hl+datagram. At each hop, routers and switches use and strip or add the headers for the layers they implement.

nodes.label: ISO/OSI Reference Model
nodes.rationale: Seven-layer model. Presentation (encryption, compression, machine-specific data meaning) and session (synchronization, checkpointing, recovery of data exchange) are absent from the Internet stack. If those services are needed they must be implemented in the application.

nodes.label: Cerf and Kahn Internetworking Principles
nodes.rationale: 1974 architecture for interconnecting networks, stated as what defines today's Internet: minimalism and autonomy so networks interconnect with no internal changes, a best-effort service model, stateless routing, and decentralized control.

nodes.label: ARPAnet
nodes.rationale: Conceived in 1967 by the Advanced Research Projects Agency; first node operational in 1969. By 1972 it had a public demo, the first host-to-host protocol NCP, the first email program, and 15 nodes. It had 200 nodes by 1979 and was decommissioned in the early 1990s. Kleinrock's 1961 queueing theory and Baran's 1964 military packet-switching work are cited as the early justification for packet switching.

nodes.label: TCP/IP
nodes.rationale: Deployed in 1983 during the proliferation of networks (CSnet, BITnet, NSFnet, Minitel), alongside SMTP (1982), DNS (1983), FTP (1985), and TCP congestion control (1988).

nodes.label: TCP Congestion Control
nodes.rationale: Packet switching can suffer excessive congestion, delay, and loss, so protocols for reliable data transfer and congestion control are required. TCP congestion control is dated to 1988.

nodes.label: Software-Defined Networking (SDN)
nodes.rationale: Dated to 2008 in the era of broadband access, 4G/5G and WiFi, provider-owned networks, cloud (Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure), and smartphones. The chapter names SDN without defining its mechanism.
